name: Mocking Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building mocking — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary mocking tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building mocking — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary mocking tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Re-check edge cases relevant to mocking (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
2. Prefer explicit, readable mocking solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
3. Measure before optimizing any mocking bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
4. Keep mocking outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
5. When mocking decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
6. State assumptions about mocking explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
7. When multiple mocking strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. Document any non-obvious mocking decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
9. Prefer the simplest mocking approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
10. Surface known limitations of a chosen mocking approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
11. When mocking guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not apply generic mocking advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not silently drop mocking edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid introducing new mocking abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for mocking, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
